paragraphs.source_en: At this point, even the passive master, who had merely been taking blows, had no choice but to fight back. The very man who had just been listening to the lecture on ethics from the sitting room with a knowing smile now sprang up, rushed out at speed, and in one stroke captured one of the students. For the master, this was indeed a remarkable victory. It was certainly a victory, but when he looked, the one he had seized was only a boy of fourteen or fifteen, hardly a fitting opponent for a bearded master. Still, the master seems to have thought this sufficient; as the boy had not apologized, he dragged him by force to the front of the veranda. Here it is necessary to say a word about the strategy adopted by the enemy. Seeing the master's fury the day before, the enemy had realized that today he would surely take the field in person. If, when that happened, some big fellow failed to escape and was caught by the master, matters would become troublesome. Therefore the best way to avoid danger was to send a first- or second-year boy to pick up the ball; even if the master caught the boy and started fussing and arguing at length, it would not affect the honor of Rakunkan. Moreover, for the master to make such a youngster his opponent would be thoroughly unbecoming of a grown man and would only deepen his disgrace. That was how the enemy had calculated it, and by ordinary human standards this was, of course, perfectly reasonable. The only thing the enemy forgot was to include in their calculations the fact that the master was no ordinary man. If the master had possessed that much common sense, he would not have rushed out yesterday either. Once a man flies into a rage, it lifts an ordinary person beyond the level of the ordinary and turns a man with common sense into one without it. Whether women or children, rickshaw men or horse drivers, so long as one can still make such distinctions, one is not yet entitled to boast of being truly beside oneself. Unless one can, like the master, capture a first-year middle-school boy not worth engaging at all and make him a hostage of war, one cannot be admitted to the ranks of the truly enraged. The pitiful one was the captive: merely obeying the orders of the upper-year students and serving as the lowly foot soldier called “ball picker,” he had the bad luck to be cornered by a senseless enemy commander, a genius of rage, and before he could even climb the fence he was detained in front of the veranda. At this, the enemy side could no longer stand by calmly and watch their comrade's disgrace, so they all vied with one another to climb over the lattice fence and burst through the side gate into the garden; there were about a dozen of them, and they lined up one after another before the master. Most wore neither jackets nor waistcoats, only white shirts with the sleeves rolled up; some stood with arms folded. Others, as a mere gesture toward clothing, had draped a faded piece of washed cotton flannel over their backs. Yet that was not true of all of them; there were also dandies wearing white canvas tops trimmed in black, with ornamental foreign letters embroidered in black across the chest. Every one of them looked like a mighty warrior capable of facing a thousand men, striking the pose of fellows who seemed to declare, “We have newly arrived from Sasayama in Tanba Province.”

paragraphs.source_en: They were all sturdy in build, blackened with sun and muscle; it seemed a waste to send them to middle school, for if men like these were made fishermen or boatmen, they would surely be of use to the nation.
